page3_img_1.png.title: C# class with one-line constructor using terse parameter names
page3_img_1.png.description: A screenshot of a small C# class declaration 'ExecutionQueryResponse : ExecutionQueryResponseBasic<QueryResults>' showing a single-line constructor: 'public ExecutionQueryResponse(QueryResults res, IReadOnlyCollection<string> str, ExecutionStepMetrics metrics) : base(res, str, metrics) { }'. The constructor uses short parameter names 'res' and 'str', performs the base(...) call on the same long line, and has an empty body formatted as '{ }'. In the paper this example is used to illustrate reviewer feedback (renaming 'res'→'queryResults' and 'str'→'queryStrings' and wrapping/indenting the constructor), and to motivate how NATURALIZE would detect and suggest such naming and formatting changes based on project conventions.

page9_img_4.png.title: Formatting suggestion accuracy vs. suggestion frequency (boxplots)
page9_img_4.png.description: Boxplots of NATURALIZE’s single-point formatting suggestion accuracy (y-axis, 0.94–1.00) plotted against suggestion frequency (x-axis, 0.0–1.0). Each box summarizes variability across the 10 evaluation projects (red line = median, box = IQR, whiskers and outliers shown); only k=1 suggestion was allowed. The median accuracy is very high (about 0.98–0.99) for a wide range of frequencies, peaking near suggestion frequency ≈0.3–0.4, and slowly declining toward ≈0.97 as frequency approaches 1.0; variability across projects and outliers increase at the highest suggestion frequencies. This supports the paper’s claim that formatting suggestions are highly accurate even when the system is asked to suggest frequently (e.g., reformatting half the whitespace).

page9_img_3.png.title: Robustness to junk identifiers: percent suggested vs percent introduced (log-log)
page9_img_3.png.description: This log-log plot shows how often NATURALIZE proposes junk (uninformative) names as the fraction of junk identifiers injected into the training corpus increases. The x-axis is the percent of identifiers in the corpus replaced with junk names (simulated low-quality corpus); the y-axis is the percent of NATURALIZE’s resulting suggestions that are junk. Each boxplot summarizes the distribution across the 10 evaluation projects (median, IQR, whiskers and outliers); the dashed line y = x marks parity between prevalence and suggestion rate. Medians lie well below the parity line and, although the suggested-junk rate rises with more junk in the corpus, NATURALIZE consistently proposes junk names at a substantially lower rate than their prevalence in the (perturbed) training data.

page4_img_1.png.title: NATURALIZE suggestion pipeline: proposers, n‑gram scoring, and top suggestions
page4_img_1.png.description: A left-to-right flowchart showing how NATURALIZE turns a code snippet under review into ranked stylistic suggestions. The pipeline: a selected “Code for Review” is passed to proposers that generate candidate edits (e.g., renaming identifiers or changing formatting), producing a small set of alternative code snippets. Those candidates are scored by a scoring function (annotated as an n-gram language model and SVM) that is trained on a project-specific Training Corpus (other code from the project) to measure each candidate’s naturalness. The highest-scoring candidates are presented as the “Top Suggestions”; the diagram emphasizes that suggestions are derived from project conventions encoded in the training corpus and ranked by statistical naturalness.

page6_img_1.png.title: Formatting tokenization of a Java method into INDENT/SPACE/ID tokens
page6_img_1.png.description: The figure shows a two-part view of a small Java snippet (lines 5–8 from TextRunnerTest.java) and the corresponding tokenization that NATURALIZE uses for learning formatting. The original source (top) is mapped (bottom) to a stream where identifiers and literals are collapsed to ID/LIT, language keywords (e.g., public, throws) remain, and whitespace is encoded as INDENT and SPACE tokens annotated with metadata (e.g., number of spaces/tabs and newlines). This representation captures both line-level indentation (INDENT with newline/indent magnitude) and intra-line spacing (SPACE or SPACE0) so an n-gram language model can learn and suggest conventional formatting.

page7_img_2.png.title: Percent of reviews vs commits mentioning conventions, naming, and formatting
page7_img_2.png.description: A small table reporting the percentage of code review threads (column “Reviews”) and commit log messages (column “Commits”) that contained feedback about coding conventions, identifier naming, and formatting, with 95% confidence intervals shown in parentheses. Results: “Conventions” occurred in 38% of reviews (31%–46%) but only 4% of commits (3%–6%); “Naming” in 24% of reviews (17%–31%) vs 1% of commits (1%–2%); and “Formatting” in 9% of reviews (6%–15%) vs 2% of commits (1%–3%). One-sided proportion tests yield p ≪ 0.01 for each row (rightmost column), indicating the differences between review feedback and commit messages are statistically significant.

page9_img_1.png.title: ROC curves of stylish? (TPR vs FPR) for identifiers and formatting
page9_img_1.png.description: A receiver-operating-characteristic plot showing true positive rate (TPR, y-axis) versus false positive rate (FPR, x-axis) for the stylish? detector under three conditions: combined (blue solid, labeled “Stylish”), formatting-only (green dotted), and identifier-only (red dashed). The curves were produced by varying the decision threshold T and show the tradeoff between catching perturbed (unnatural) snippets and avoiding false rejections; the combined detector dominates the others across most thresholds. Notably, at a low FPR of ~0.05 the combined stylish? detector still achieves about 40% TPR (i.e., correctly rejects ~40% of perturbed snippets), and formatting perturbations are easier to detect than identifier perturbations (formatting curve lies above the identifier curve at lower FPRs).

page3_img_2.png.title: Devstyle Eclipse plugin rename suggestions for parameter 'each'
page3_img_2.png.description: The screenshot shows the devstyle Eclipse plugin offering renaming suggestions for the parameter named "each" in the method signature private Test testCaseForClass(Class<?> each) (the token is highlighted in the editor and its occurrences are emphasized). A small dialog lists ranked alternatives with confidence percentages — "testClass (31.8%)", "klass (25.4%)", and "returnType (22.4%)" — along with Cancel/OK controls. These percentages are the NATURALIZE language model’s naturalness/confidence scores computed from the project corpus; accepting a suggestion would apply a scoped rename of that identifier across its uses, as the paper describes for the devstyle tool.

page8_img_1.png.title: Identifier suggestion accuracy vs. suggestion frequency (variables, calls, typenames)
page8_img_1.png.description: Three side-by-side line plots comparing NATURALIZE’s top-k suggestion accuracy (y-axis) against suggestion frequency (x-axis) for (a) variables, (b) method calls, and (c) typenames. Each plot shows two curves: solid for k=1 and dashed for k=5, with shaded bands indicating the interquartile range across the 10 evaluation projects; each plotted point corresponds to a different confidence threshold t that controls how often the system makes suggestions. All three plots show the same trend: accuracy falls as the system is forced to suggest more often, and allowing k=5 alternatives substantially improves the chance the true name appears in the list. Typenames are predicted most accurately (near 0.98–1.0 at low suggestion frequency, declining to ~0.85–0.90 at high frequency), variables are intermediate (≈0.98 down to ≈0.70 for k=1; higher for k=5), and method calls are the hardest (≈0.95 down to ≈0.50 for k=1, with k=5 remaining notably better).

page9_img_2.png.title: Preservation of surprising (UNK) identifier names vs suggestion threshold
page9_img_2.png.description: Line chart plotting the percentage of ‘‘surprising’’ identifiers (those mapped to the UNK token during training) that NATURALIZE leaves unchanged as the suggestion-confidence threshold t varies. The x‑axis is the threshold t (controlling how aggressively the system makes suggestions) and the y‑axis is the percent of UNK names preserved; the legend shows three curves: solid=variables, dashed=methods, dotted=types. As t increases (the system becomes more conservative), the preservation rate rises toward 100% for all identifier kinds; types are preserved at a higher rate than variables and methods across the range. Shaded bands around each curve show variability across the evaluated projects (interquartile range), and at the authors’ chosen operating regime NATURALIZE preserves the large majority of surprising names (i.e., only a small fraction of UNK identifiers receive non‑UNK suggestions), demonstrating the sympathetic uniqueness principle.
